. Instead of jumping in with solutions, David guides the conversation using key coaching questions. The conversation closes with Sarah identifying what was most useful: realizing the real challenge and feeling empowered to handle it differently.

text.val:
SCENARIO: “The Overwhelmed Team Member”

How coaching shifts the conversation from fixing → thinking.

Context:
Sarah, a project coordinator, walks into her manager David’s office looking tense. She’s juggling multiple deadlines and feels like everything is slipping. David is known for being helpful — maybe too helpful — and his instinct is to jump in and rescue the situation.

Here’s how this scenario typically plays out in many teams (the “old way”), followed by the coaching version (the Coaching Habit way).

🔴 The Old Way (Advice Trap Activated)

Sarah:
“I’m drowning. The reporting deadline moved up again. I can’t keep up.”

David (fixer mode):
“Okay, let’s reorganize your tasks. Show me your priority list. I can take the reporting off your plate for now, and maybe the team can pick up some of your admin tasks.”

Sarah:
“…That would help, thanks.”

What actually happened?

Sarah didn’t clarify the real issue.

David took work he shouldn’t own.

Sarah becomes more dependent.

David becomes more overwhelmed.

No one learned anything that prevents this from happening again.

This is how the vicious cycle continues.

🟢 The Coaching Habit Way (Curiosity Activated)

Here’s how the same situation looks when David uses coaching instead of fixing.

STEP 1 — The Kickstart Question

David:
“Sure, Sarah — what’s on your mind?”

Sarah:
“I feel overwhelmed, and the reporting deadline was moved up again.”

STEP 2 — The AWE Question

David:
“Got it. And what else?”

Sarah:
“…Well, honestly, I don’t think the team is clear about who owns what. Everything ends up on my plate.”

STEP 3 — The Focus Question

David:
“Okay. What’s the real challenge here for you?”

Sarah:
“…I think the real issue is that I’m not pushing back when work gets delegated. I just keep saying yes.”

Now we’re getting somewhere.

STEP 4 — The Foundation Question

David:
“That makes sense. What do you want in this situation?”

Sarah:
“I want clearer boundaries and a more sustainable workload.”

STEP 5 — The Lazy Question

David:
“So, how can I help?”

Sarah:
“I don’t need you to take anything off my plate — I need help setting expectations with the team.”

Perfect.
She’s not asking for rescue — she’s asking for empowerment.

STEP 6 — The Strategic Question

David:
“If you say yes to clearer boundaries, what might you need to say no to?”

Sarah:
“…Probably my habit of saying yes automatically. And the fear of disappointing someone.”

STEP 7 — The Learning Question

David:
“This was a great conversation. What was most useful for you?”

Sarah:
“Realizing that the workload isn’t the issue — it’s my lack of boundaries. I feel lighter already.”

This is a coaching conversation.
Short, simple, and transformative.
She grows.
He leads.
The problem becomes clear — and solvable.

SCENARIO: “The Overwhelmed Team Member”

How coaching shifts the conversation from fixing → thinking.

text.val: Which Coaching Habit question would not have been helpful in this scenario?
What’s on your mind?
And what else?
What’s the real challenge here for you?
Why can’t you manage your workload better?
What did Sarah identify as the most useful part of the conversation?
Learning a new reporting tool
Realizing that the workload wasn’t the root issue
Being offered a temporary assistant
Being reassigned to a new project
What shift does the scenario illustrate about coaching?
Coaching means leaders do less listening and more talking
Coaching is about giving the best advice possible
Coaching helps people uncover deeper issues and take ownership
Coaching works only in formal performance reviews
What mistake would David have made if he followed his old instinct?
Ignoring Sarah’s feelings completely
Giving her more tasks to build resilience
Asking her to lead a separate project
Jumping in to fix the problem for her
How did David empower Sarah rather than rescue her?
He assigned her fewer projects
He gave her detailed instructions for fixing the issue
He asked questions that helped her reflect and decide
He suggested she delegate her tasks to others immediately
What was the real challenge Sarah uncovered during the conversation?
A. She lacked the technical skills to meet the deadline
She didn’t have enough support from leadership
She wasn’t setting boundaries and kept saying yes to everything
The team was refusing to help her with tasks
What did Sarah ultimately say she wanted?
A complete break from all responsibilities
A promotion to avoid day-to-day tasks
Clearer boundaries and a more manageable workload
A different manager to work with
Which behavior did David avoid because he used a coaching approach?
Micromanaging Sarah’s project timeline
Asking clarifying questions
Listening actively
Taking on Sarah’s tasks himself
Why is the Strategic Question important in this scenario?
It helps the leader assign work more quickly
It forces Sarah to admit she can’t do the job
It allows the leader to choose priorities unilaterally
It clarifies the tradeoffs behind saying yes
Which question helped Sarah open up beyond her first answer?
“And what else?”
“Why didn’t you plan ahead?”
“Are you sure you can’t handle it?”
“Do you want me to take this over?”
